steps.user_message: I want to file my 2023 taxes correctly. I'm head of household in Phoenix AZ. W-2 from Midwest Health Systems: $82,350. Additional income: $15,000 (consulting, 2 clients), $890 from Citi savings, $480 from Fidelity. Home office: 155 sq ft exclusive; I pay $2,050/month for 780 sq ft. Deductions: $2,700 student loan interest (MOHELA, 2016–2019); $800 to St. Mary's Food Bank (have the receipt) with receipt; $1,350 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — I ran the numbers from what you provided and laid out what you can (and can’t) deduct, which filing method will almost certainly be better, how to treat the home office, and the IRS forms you’ll need.

Summary conclusion (short)
- Take the Head-of-Household standard deduction for 2023 ($20,800). Your likely itemized deductions (~$800 charity only) are far below the standard deduction.
- Report your consulting income on Schedule C, take a home-office business expense (actual method will likely give a bigger deduction than the simplified method), pay/report self-employment tax (Schedule SE) and claim half of that as an adjustment to income.
- The student-loan interest deduction is very likely NOT available because your MAGI is above the phaseout range for 2023.
- You may be able to claim the 20% Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction on your Schedule C income — use Form 8995 to calculate.

Detailed walk-through and numbers
1) Income to report
- W‑2 wages: $82,350 (Midwest Health Systems) — reported on Form 1040.
- Consulting income (self‑employment): $15,000 — reported on Schedule C (and Schedule SE for SE tax).
- Interest: $890 (Citi) + $480 (Fidelity) = $1,370 — report on Form 1040 (Schedule B not required unless taxable interest > $1,500).

2) Home office
- Space: 155 sq ft exclusive use; home is 780 sq ft. Business percentage = 155 / 780 ≈ 19.87%.
- Rent: $2,050/month → annual rent $24,600. Business portion of rent = 24,600 × 19.87% ≈ $4,887.
- Two methods:
  - Simplified: $5 × 155 sq ft = $775.
  - Actual: your apportioned share of rent (≈ $4,887) and a proportional share of other allowable expenses (utilities, renters insurance, etc., if you have them). Based only on the rent you gave, actual method gives a much larger deduction than the simplified method.
- How to claim: For a self-employed consultant you claim the home-office expense on Schedule C as a business expense (either using the simplified box or the actual expenses line items). Keep documentation showing exclusive use, measurement, rent/utility bills, and how you computed the percentage.

3) Business expenses and self-employment tax
- Business expenses you listed: $1,350 (unreimbursed expenses) — treated as Schedule C expenses (these reduce self-employment net profit).
- If you use the actual home-office method, add the home-office portion of rent (~$4,887) to your Schedule C expenses.
- Rough estimated Schedule C net profit (illustrative):
  - Gross consulting revenue: $15,000
  - Less unreimbursed/business expenses: $1,350
  - Less home-office portion of rent (actual method): $4,887
  - Net profit ≈ $8,763
- Self-employment (SE) tax approx:
  - SE tax base = 92.35% × net profit ≈ 0.9235 × 8,763 ≈ $8,090
  - SE tax (15.3%) ≈ $8,090 × 0.153 ≈ $1,238
  - You can deduct half of SE tax as an adjustment to income on Schedule 1 (≈ $619). That reduces your AGI.

4) Student loan interest (MOHELA, $2,700)
- The student loan interest deduction is an above-the-line deduction up to $2,500 but phases out by MAGI.
- For 2023 the phaseout for single/head‑of‑household filers begins around $75,000 and is fully phased out at $90,000 MAGI.
- Your approximate MAGI before the student loan interest deduction (W-2 + consulting + interest) is about $98,720, and after subtracting the half-SE-tax adjustment it’s still ≈ $98,100 — above the $90,000 cutoff.
- Conclusion: you almost certainly cannot take the student-loan interest deduction for 2023 given the income you listed.

(If you have other above‑the‑line deductions not listed — e.g., a deductible traditional IRA contribution, deductible self‑employed retirement plan contribution, or SEP/SIMPLE contribution — those can reduce MAGI and could change eligibility. Consider those only if appropriate.)

5) Charitable contribution ($800 to St. Mary’s Food Bank)
- For 2023 there is no universal above-the-line charitable deduction for non-itemizers. So that $800 is deductible only if you itemize.
- Your likely itemized deductions (from data you gave) are about $800 — far below the Head‑of‑Household standard deduction ($20,800). So take the standard deduction and do not claim that $800 on federal return.
- Keep the receipt (you have it); you will need it if you ever itemize or for substantiation.

6) Itemize vs standard
- Standard deduction for Head of Household in 2023 = $20,800.
- Likely itemized deductions from what you told me = $800 (charity). Unless you have other significant deductible items (mortgage interest, large state+local taxes up to $10k limit, big medical expenses above 7.5% of AGI, etc.), standard deduction is better. So choose standard deduction.

7) Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction
- Because you have net profit from a sole proprietorship (Schedule C), you may qualify for a QBI deduction up to 20% of your qualified business income.
- Rough QBI estimate = net Schedule C profit ≈ $8,763 → 20% ≈ $1,750. This is a below-the-line deduction (Form 8995 or 8995-A) and reduces taxable income (not AGI).
- Because your taxable income (after standard deduction) is well below the QBI phaseout threshold for specified service businesses (2023 threshold ≈ $182,100), you are likely eligible for the full 20% QBI for this small consulting income. Use Form 8995 to compute exactly.

8) Forms you’ll need (federal)
- Form 1040 (federal individual return).
- Schedule 1 (for adjustments — e.g., half of SE tax goes here).
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — report consulting income and business expenses, including home-office deduction.
- Schedule SE — compute self-employment tax.
- Form 8995 (or 8995-A) — to compute the QBI deduction (if you claim it).
- 1099‑NEC / 1099‑MISC: report consulting income even if you didn’t receive 1099s.
- 1099‑INT: report the $890 and $480 interest amounts (you should receive 1099‑INTs).
- Schedule B only if total taxable interest > $1,500 (yours totals $1,370 → not required).
- Keep your charitable receipt (substantiation) in case you ever itemize or for audit records.

9) State filing (Arizona)
- You’ll need to file Arizona state income tax (Form 140 for residents) and report the same federal income, with Arizona adjustments as required. Arizona rules differ somewhat; consider state-specific guidance or a tax preparer familiar with AZ filing.

10) Practical action items / recommendations
- Use Schedule C and claim the actual home-office deduction (rent portion) because it looks larger than the simplified method given the numbers you provided. Keep documentation (square footage, exclusive-use statement, rent receipts, utilities).
- Report the consulting income and the business expenses (unreimbursed expenses) on Schedule C.
- Pay any estimated taxes for 2024 (quarterly Form 1040-ES) if you expect similar self-employment income so you avoid underpayment penalties.
- Save receipts: home-office documentation, receipts for the $800 charitable gift (you said you have it), business expense receipts, and student loan payment records.
- Consider (if you want to reduce taxable/MAGI in future years) options such as tax-deductible retirement plan contributions (SEP IRA, Solo 401(k), or deductible Traditional IRA if eligible) — these can reduce AGI and potentially change eligibility for some deductions. Consult a tax pro for personalized planning.

Caveats and offer to help further
- I used only the items you listed and estimated the home-office allocation and SE tax roughly. Exact numbers change with additional allowable business expenses, other income, retirement plan contributions, or other adjustments.
- If you want, I can:
  - prepare a more precise estimate (I’ll need any other income, W-2 withholding, any additional expenses, state tax withheld, retirement contributions, etc.),
  - draft the Schedule C entries (wording for descriptions and amounts) or
  - walk you through filling out each required form step-by-step.

Would you like me to estimate exact tax owed/refund (including computing QBI, federal income tax, and SE tax) using the numbers you gave? If so, tell me whether to use the actual home‑office method (I used it above) or the simplified method.
